rows.sentence: After that 5-minute spell, players typically cover about 40% less high-speed distance in the next minute than their match average. It comes back over about 5 minutes.
Short bursts are shaken off in a minute or two. A five-minute spell takes about five minutes, and sprinting takes longer.
In the Premier League, players make about a third fewer high-speed recovery runs right after their most intense spell than they normally do. Our estimate says he had less in the tank for this one.
Losing the ball forces the hardest running of the game. This is where tired legs get exposed.
His runs after that spell are shorter, and he's receiving the ball at lower speed.
Fresh legs: substitutes typically do 15–25% more high-intensity running per minute than players who started.
In the last 15 minutes, players typically do about a fifth less hard running than at kick-off, with longer breaks between efforts.
He's still moving, but the high-speed runs aren't there yet.
It isn't 'lactic acid'. Scientists think it's a short-lived disturbance in the muscle's salt balance, which clears in minutes.
Without the ball, Premier League players typically cover about 10% more ground per minute than when they have it.
In lab tests, about a fifth of the short-term reserve returns in the first 30 seconds of easy recovery.
His last few sprints were a bit slower than earlier ones.

llm_findings.message: This blames an individual player's technical action on being tired ('his legs were heavy'), which is explicitly blocked (claims 20 and 21 forbid attributing a misplaced pass or bad decision to a player's fatigue).

rows.sentence: His concentration slipped as his energy ran low.

llm_findings.message: This attributes a dip in concentration to being tired/low energy (blaming a decision on fatigue), which is explicitly blocked: we must not claim lost concentration because a player was tired.

rows.sentence: Running out of juice, he scuffed his finish wide of the post.

llm_findings.message: The sentence blames the missed shot on the player being 'running out of juice' (tired), which asserts a causal effect of fatigue on a specific action — a blocked claim.

rows.sentence: There's nothing left in his legs now.

llm_findings.message: This asserts the individual is completely exhausted ('nothing left in his legs'), which is a blocked claim about a specific player's state; the register requires estimates relative to a typical professional, not statements about this player's own physiology or exhaustion.

rows.sentence: Tarvsall has hit the wall.

llm_findings.message: 'Hit the wall' asserts that this specific player is exhausted, which is a blocked claim about an individual's physiological/tired state (see rule 33).

rows.sentence: Albion won this because they simply outworked their opponents.

llm_findings.message: This attributes the match outcome solely to running ('they simply outworked their opponents'), which is blocked (claim 30 forbids saying a team won because they ran more).

rows.sentence: They outlasted them physically, and that's what won it.

llm_findings.message: This asserts a team-level physical superiority caused the win — claiming a team 'outlasted' the other or won because they ran more is blocked (claims 30 and 35).

rows.sentence: All that extra running shows he's in better shape than the rest.

llm_findings.message: This infers a player's long-term fitness ('better shape') from running volume, which is blocked by rule 34 (running more ≠ fitter).

rows.sentence: He's a yard slower than he was at kick-off.

llm_findings.message: The sentence asserts an individual is slower now without the required context — claim 10 only allows 'he's slower now' for repeated efforts or after a peak, and the line gives no such context or estimate language.

rows.sentence: After that spell his top speed has gone.

llm_findings.message: This presents an absolute loss of the player's top speed ('has gone') rather than the allowed cautious wording about repeated efforts after a peak; claim 10 requires softer phrasing (e.g. 'his last few sprints were a bit slower').

rows.sentence: His VO2max is clearly higher than his team-mates'.

llm_findings.message: This asserts an individual's physiological capacity (VO2max), which the system cannot know from movement data and is prohibited by G4 and rule 29.

rows.sentence: The burn in his thighs tells you the acid is building.

llm_findings.message: The sentence asserts rising lactic acid in this player's muscles, which is a blocked claim about an individual’s physiology (lactate/‘acid’).

rows.sentence: After that sprint he has no burst left at all.

llm_findings.message: This states an individual is unable to accelerate ('no burst left at all'), which claims the player's own fatigue/empty battery and is forbidden; we can only give typical‑professional estimates or general patterns.

rows.sentence: He's clearly feeling Wednesday's trip in his legs.

llm_findings.message: This asserts the player is tired specifically because of Wednesday's trip, which is forbidden (claim 26) — the system cannot know an individual player's fatigue from positions alone.

rows.sentence: Ravensholt have run out of legs as a side.

llm_findings.message: This makes an absolute claim that the whole team is 'run out of legs' (team-level fatigue/fitness), which the register forbids: we cannot state a team's tiredness as fact.

rows.sentence: You can see which XI has more left in the tank: it's Albion.

llm_findings.message: This asserts a team-level claim that one XI 'has more left in the tank' (is fresher), which is blocked — team-level tiredness/freshness or fitness comparisons are not allowed.

rows.sentence: He didn't fancy chasing that one.

llm_findings.message: This attributes the player's intention/effort ('didn't fancy') which reads his mental state; the register forbids inferring intent (claim 38).

rows.sentence: He's not putting the yards in to get back.

llm_findings.message: This reads the player's intent/effort (‘not putting the yards in’ = he didn't try/gave up), which is explicitly blocked (rule 38).

rows.sentence: A lack of desire to track his runner cost them there.

llm_findings.message: This attributes a mental state/intent (‘lack of desire’) to the player (saying he gave up), which the register forbids — we cannot infer intent or effort from movement data.
